episode_title: What Motorsport Can Teach Us About Staying Ahead
question: How did asbestos brake pads dominate motorsport racing before regulation changes in the early 1990s?
transcript_excerpt: The best brake pads in the industry, which everyone wants to use, were asbestos. Matt Neal and other racers used to go around buying as many of these pads as possible because they were so much better than anything else in the industry. They got banned in about early nineties, after which technology and research moved the industry forward to safer alternatives.

episode_title: What Motorsport Can Teach Us About Staying Ahead
question: What is the economic size of classic racing in Europe and how is it positioned relative to modern racing regulations?
transcript_excerpt: Classic racing in Europe is a billion euro industry. It is a bit more insulated from the green net zero agenda even though manufacturers are making efforts with sustainable fuels and sustainable materials on the tires. This growing side of the industry excited Matt Neal as a new opportunity for Team Dynamics.

episode_title: What Motorsport Can Teach Us About Staying Ahead
question: Why did Honda withdraw from British Touring Car Championship sponsorship after 17 years due to EU regulations?
transcript_excerpt: Honda stopped sponsoring touring cars because EU net zero CAF regulations require them to pay fines of approximately £6,000 to sell a Type R in the UK. Since they did not want to sell Type Rs on the road, there was no product to promote through touring car racing, making the sponsorship no longer commercially viable for brand exercise purposes.

episode_title: What Motorsport Can Teach Us About Staying Ahead
question: How has AI-driven data analysis transformed motorsport driver performance analysis in the last 18 months?
transcript_excerpt: AI has taken a big leap in the last 18 months, allowing teams to analyze video footage of cars on track from TV broadcasts and extract data about performance. Without any insight into the workings of the car, AI can tell how much horsepower a car is running, when it is on boost or off boost, and where the car is quick on track.

episode_title: What Motorsport Can Teach Us About Staying Ahead
question: What was the competitive disadvantage for privateer touring car teams using different tire specifications compared to factory teams in the 1990s?
transcript_excerpt: In the 1990s, tire wars meant that whichever manufacturer had the contract that year would win, making it unfair for privateer teams. A two-car works team would use 200 tires a weekend compared to modern teams allowed 16 new tires and 8 used ones per car per weekend. When Matt Neal's team was finally allowed to run the same spec tires as factory cars, they won their first race.
